narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 61.5% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the model judged failure more likely than passing, so the school treated the risk as too high for admission. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile: you were in decile 2, while accepted students averaged about 5.79, and this low relative standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. Although your score of 37 was very close to the accepted average of 37.18, it acted as a counterweight toward passing. The third factor was your first-year class-rank decile: at 3, compared with an accepted average of 6, it also pushed toward failure. Together, the two low class-rank indicators outweighed the LSAT counterweight.

To proceed, ask admissions for feedback, meet an academic advisor, and build a concrete improvement plan. Focus on strengthening your academic record, consider LSAT preparation or retaking only if practice scores show real gains, and reapply when you can show improved evidence of bar readiness.
